title: The Three Acts Of A Mathematical Story
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer republishes an early article proposing that a math task should be structured like a film in three acts, with his own retrospective commentary on what has and has not held up. Act One introduces a central conflict visually and viscerally with as little language and math demanded as possible. Act Two has students overcome obstacles by finding resources and developing tools, and Act Three resolves the conflict and sets up a sequel or extension problem. His conclusion is that teachers who see Act Two as their whole job are mistaken, and that their value lies in motivating the second act and paying it off. In the commentary he flags that his Act Two thinking was under-opinionated and his predictions about adaptive software and flipped classrooms were a miss, while the core conviction about sensory intuition and a feeling of resolution endures.
points: Math lessons can borrow story structure: a clear visual conflict, a middle where students gather tools, and a payoff.
Act One should ask little and offer a lot, imposing minimal demands of language or math.
Many teachers treat Act Two (worked examples and practice) as the job, yet that is the part students can get elsewhere.
Resolution should feel earned rather than hidden in the back of the teacher's edition, with extension problems ready as the sequel.
Meyer's commentary candidly marks what aged badly, such as his faith in Khan Academy and adaptive software.
quotes: One of the major identity crises of my young adulthood was the fact that I had an abundance of interest in screenwriting, directing, and storytelling and very little talent for it. Meanwhile, you could flip that relationship for math teaching. I graduated university with a math degree, headed into math teaching, and fretted about this constantly in my early twenties.
Introduce the central conflict of your story/task clearly, visually, viscerally, using as few words as possible.
Leave no one out of your first act. Your first act should impose as few demands on the students as possible – either of language or of math. It should ask for little and offer a lot.
That what it’s like for students to encounter the resolution of their conflict in the back of the teacher’s edition of the textbook.

Going forward, the value you bring to your math classroom increasingly will be tied up in the first and third acts of mathematical storytelling, your ability to motivate the second act and then pay off on that hard work.
